question: Does stronger AdamW weight decay improve generalization and the useful ensemble contribution of our proven ConvNeXt-Tiny representation?
primary_intervention: AdamW weight decay0.0001->0.05, same original parameter groups including norm/bias
comparability: Historical S06 cohort, ImageNet weights, architecture/head, seed,224,flip,weightedCE,effective32,AdamW/LRs/raw-accuracy LR scheduling are preserved. Planned optimizer intervention: decay0.0001->0.05 on the original parameter groups (including norm/bias). Engineering amendment: guarded FP32 validation instead of historical AMP; this can change selection/scheduler trajectories, so this is not a pure causal weight-decay estimate. Seed/runtime alone do not reproduce the old trajectory.
initialization: Same fresh cached ImageNet1k initialization as S06; full-network fine-tuning, not a resume of an overfit HAM10000 checkpoint
cbam: S95 has no added attention; existing CBAM member and all S83 sources are preserved
stop_policy: One20-epoch window; raw accuracy/F1 winners and cumulative meaningful counters independent; no automatic next GPU or ensemble run
future_ensemble: After user returns: use the standalone macro-F1 winner for one S83 six-member replacement of original S06 Tiny; original CBAM member retained; equal1/6 unchanged. No weight/checkpoint sweep.
compute_estimate: 15–30minutes, estimated2–3GiB peak total process VRAM; historical S06 peak allocated1.5GiB, approximately42seconds/epoch late in training
regularization_scope: A generalization hypothesis, not CPU-verified accuracy. With unchanged small LRs, maximum pure-decay-only shrink at constant starting LR is about0.655% backbone and2.17% head over4380updates; scheduler reductions make it smaller. A500-fold coefficient change is not a500-fold model change.
source_scope: Official ImageNet training defaults AdamW decay0.05; not a HAM10000 result or proof of an optimal fine-tuning setting. Our original group membership is retained rather than copying official norm/bias exclusion or the entire recipe.
